shortlist.title: The life archive inside a whale’s ear
shortlist.centralQuestion: What can layered whale earwax reveal about a life no one watched?
shortlist.whyCare: An unlikely museum object could preserve observations across a life that researchers could not continuously watch.
shortlist.payoff: Understand how a physical sequence can become a time-indexed biological archive.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: A wax cross-section, paired layers and a cautiously labeled chemical timeline; no imagined memories or whale emotions.
shortlist.principalRisk: Layer-to-time mapping varies by species; hormones are proxies, not a diary of feelings. The 2016 article’s one-analyzed-plug wording is historical, not a current field count. Collections involve dead whales and whaling history.
shortlist.evidencePath: Smithsonian’s object account leads to Usenko/Trumble’s primary earplug chemistry work and later methodological studies; check dating, sample scope and contamination.
shortlist.historyComparison: Ocean Depth shares ocean context; Wood Frog shares biology. Neither reconstructs life through an archival specimen. Avoid a maritime continuation from Longitude or a survival spectacle.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Odd stored object → successive layers → dated chemical measurements → what a life archive can and cannot tell us.
researchRequirements: Retrieve primary earplug studies, sample numbers and dating assumptions.
Separate contaminant/hormone measurements from causal or emotional interpretation.
Check species scope and lawful original/licensed specimen depiction.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Finalist: strong evidence-detective story; marine adjacency is a real portfolio tradeoff, not a disqualification.
preliminaryHooks: Why would a museum keep a whale’s earwax?
What could this wax preserve from a life no one watched?

shortlist.title: The painting that makes sense from the side
shortlist.centralQuestion: How does a distorted shape in The Ambassadors resolve into a skull?
shortlist.whyCare: A confusing mark becomes legible when the observer changes position.
shortlist.payoff: Understand anamorphosis as a relationship between image and viewpoint, with historical meaning kept distinct from geometry.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Compare front and oblique viewing, then a simple original perspective construction. The known artwork can anchor the explanation if reproduction rights permit.
shortlist.principalRisk: Do not fake the gallery viewing angle or confuse moving the viewer with magically changing paint. Original painting age does not clear every museum photograph. Symbolic interpretation and exact construction method are qualified.
shortlist.evidencePath: National Gallery object record and 2024 scholarly catalogue; later test projective geometry and confirm reproduction terms.
shortlist.historyComparison: No completed art story; differs from Earth to Stars/Speed of Light scale and Longitude’s time-to-position mechanism. Cycle #2’s unproduced Magritte idea is paint-layer conservation, not viewpoint.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Unresolved shape → changed viewing position → distortion resolves → explain perspective; optional bounded historical meaning.
researchRequirements: Check an actual viewing geometry and reproducible geometric example.
Distinguish documented object facts from inferred artist method/meaning.
Resolve a public-domain, original or licensed reproduction route.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Finalist: especially immediate visual payoff; rights and honest viewpoint depiction are decisive.
preliminaryHooks: Why does this painting make sense from the side?
The paint stays still. What changes when you move?

shortlist.title: Same choice, different blame
shortlist.centralQuestion: Should an outcome outside your control change how people judge your choice?
shortlist.whyCare: Many people recognize tension between judging a choice and judging what happened.
shortlist.payoff: Name resultant moral luck and understand why responsibility, blame and moral worth can be distinguished; no promised settled answer.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Two explicitly hypothetical people make the same careless choice but encounter different outcomes; compare control and consequence without graphic harm.
shortlist.principalRisk: This is a philosophical argument, not an empirical claim about everybody’s psychology or a legal rule. Avoid outrage, a loaded tragedy or claiming philosophers resolved the dilemma. Hypotheticals need exactly matched choices.
shortlist.evidencePath: Stanford Encyclopedia’s current Moral Luck entry maps Williams/Nagel and responses; retrieve the original arguments only after selection.
shortlist.historyComparison: New philosophical domain among completed videos. No traffic scenario is needed despite Phantom Traffic; not the Cycle #1 identity paradox or voting cycle.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Matched choice → different outcome → conflicting judgments → distinguish what was controlled from what resulted, leaving a fair question.
researchRequirements: Read Williams/Nagel and representative objections.
Check hypothetical symmetry and distinguish types of judgment.
Keep legal liability and empirical moral psychology outside scope unless separately sourced.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Finalist: intellectual and discussion payoff with genuinely different story shape; requires clarity without false resolution.
preliminaryHooks: Same careless choice. Different outcome. Same blame?
How much of a judgment should depend on luck?

shortlist.title: Why melted chocolate can come back wrong
shortlist.centralQuestion: Why can the same chocolate become glossy and snappy—or dull and soft?
shortlist.whyCare: People can recognize the difference in a familiar food without knowing what changed inside it.
shortlist.payoff: Understand that composition alone does not determine chocolate texture: crystal arrangement and thermal history matter.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Compare identical-composition samples with different finish/fracture, then a bounded crystal-arrangement explanation. Opportunities only; no medium or treatment selected.
shortlist.principalRisk: The museum activity is a starting lead, not sufficient polymorph evidence. Distinguish fat bloom from sugar bloom and cocoa-butter forms from particle-size effects; avoid universal recipes or implying every chocolate formulation behaves alike.
shortlist.evidencePath: Exploratorium activity plus cocoa-butter polymorphism/tempering research and authoritative food-science sources; later check formulations, form transitions and texture evidence.
shortlist.historyComparison: First completed food story if selected. Wood Frog uses temperature in physiology, but this is food/material structure; Human Engineering is structure scale, not phase history. No old renderer advantage.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Same chocolate, different result → melting erases useful structure → controlled crystallization changes the finish/fracture → thermal history explains the difference.
researchRequirements: Locate primary cocoa-butter polymorphism/tempering literature.
Separate composition, crystal form, cooling history and bloom mechanisms.
Scope sample comparison and any schematic; do not invent a measured demonstration.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Advisory proposed advance: familiar tactile question, substantial understanding shift and a new food/material angle. Primary evidence must still be obtained after owner selection.
preliminaryHooks: Why can the same chocolate come back wrong after melting?
What changes when the ingredients stay the same?

shortlist.title: Shared does not have to mean ruined
shortlist.centralQuestion: What lets some communities sustain a resource they all use?
shortlist.whyCare: A common fatalistic story about shared resources can be replaced with a conditional explanation about rules.
shortlist.payoff: Understand why commons outcomes depend on institutions, monitoring and circumstances, rather than ownership labels alone.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: One later documented resource case; show users, access rules and observable consequences, distinguishing governed commons from open access.
shortlist.principalRisk: Nobel summaries can overstate “disproved.” Shared resources do not always succeed; no one-rule cure, political prescription or universal policy claim. Primary lecture access failed; case selection remains open.
shortlist.evidencePath: Nobel 2009 summary and Ostrom lecture/Governing the Commons lead to case studies; later compare a bounded documented case and failure conditions.
shortlist.historyComparison: Billion Dollars is monetary scale; Phantom Traffic is flow dynamics. This is institutional cooperation and conditional human agency, not another self-organizing simulation.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Shared resource creates a dilemma → identify actual use rules → monitoring/coordination changes incentives → conditional outcome, not an inevitable tragedy or miracle.
researchRequirements: Retrieve Ostrom’s primary text through an accessible legitimate route.
Choose one documented case and check outcomes, boundaries and failure conditions.
Distinguish open access from governed commons and illustration from observation.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Finalist: meaningful social/institutional diversification; primary access and a compact case are unresolved.
preliminaryHooks: Does sharing a resource have to ruin it?
What changes when the people sharing it can make rules?

shortlist.title: When a recording became something you could copy
shortlist.centralQuestion: How did flat-disc recording help turn a performance into a mass-produced object?
shortlist.whyCare: A recorded performance becomes a reproducible physical product rather than a singular event.
shortlist.payoff: Understand the connection between recording format, copying and distribution without claiming one inventor did everything.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Follow one performance to a groove/master and multiple copies; historically scoped mechanical stages and labels.
shortlist.principalRisk: Avoid implying cylinders could never be copied or that all disc manufacture used one method. Archives and old recordings have item-specific rights; patent chronology and collaborators matter.
shortlist.evidencePath: Library of Congress Berliner collection and its patent/manuscript leads; direct collection open failed, indexed description is available. Later retrieve primary manufacturing records.
shortlist.historyComparison: No completed recording or media-industry story. Differs from Human Engineering’s giant structures and Cycle #1’s unproduced Foley; some human invention shape adjacency to Longitude.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Performance → physical trace → reproducible disc → distribution consequence, with preceding/competing technology acknowledged.
researchRequirements: Check recording versus duplication stages and chronology.
Compare actual cylinder/disc copying practices without absolute claims.
Clear archive sound/object rights or use original explanation.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Shortlist reserve: strong cultural technology link; object and chronology risks make it less ready than final five.
preliminaryHooks: How did one performance become thousands of physical copies?

shortlist.title: The cocoa powder made for laboratories
shortlist.centralQuestion: Why would a measurement institute make a cocoa reference material?
shortlist.whyCare: A familiar pantry substance has an unfamiliar laboratory role.
shortlist.payoff: Understand a reference material as a check on a measurement method, with uncertainty and matrix effects.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Unknown sample, known reference and comparison; distinguish the reference powder from a universal ideal cocoa.
shortlist.principalRisk: Do not turn cocoa flavanols into health claims or imply a standard guarantees a product’s quality. A numerical example could confuse calibration with validation. No current price or availability asserted.
shortlist.evidencePath: NIST’s 2021 cocoa reference article leads to the specific material certificate and value-assignment documentation; later check intended uses and uncertainties.
shortlist.historyComparison: No laboratory reference story. Shares food with chocolate candidate, but purpose is trust in measurement, not texture; only one food story is in final five.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Laboratories disagree or need a check → characterized reference → compare the method → trust has an explicit uncertainty.
researchRequirements: Inspect certificate and intended use of the exact cocoa material.
Distinguish calibration, method validation and health inference.
Check any illustrative result against an internally consistent example.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Shortlist reserve: excellent odd-object question; abstract payoff and food overlap reduce finalist diversity.
preliminaryHooks: Why would a measurement institute make cocoa powder?

shortlist.title: The flowers inside a fig
shortlist.centralQuestion: How can a fig contain flowers you never see from the outside?
shortlist.whyCare: An ordinary fruit invites a reveal of an unfamiliar internal structure.
shortlist.payoff: Recognize a fig’s enclosed flowering structure and why pollination depends on species/cultivar.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: An anatomically accurate cutaway and scoped pollination relationship, avoiding a gross-out insect reveal.
shortlist.principalRisk: Avoid “every fig contains a wasp.” Edible cultivars and pollination vary; imagery must not place all flowers or reproductive structures incorrectly. Kew open returned 403.
shortlist.evidencePath: Kew Ficus carica lead plus later botanical morphology and fig–wasp/cultivar research.
shortlist.historyComparison: New plant anatomy among completed content; biology adjacency to Wood Frog but a reproductive relationship rather than freeze survival. Different from ocean and navigational history.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Familiar fig → enclosed flowers → how pollination can work → qualify species/cultivar differences.
researchRequirements: Retrieve botanical morphology and named cultivar pollination evidence.
Check obligate relations versus cultivated exceptions.
Clear original/CC0 specimen imagery and accurate cutaway.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Shortlist reserve: accessible reveal but meme misconceptions and access limits need care.

shortlist.title: How a language begins between people
shortlist.centralQuestion: How does shared signing develop structure across a new community?
shortlist.whyCare: A language can be studied as a community’s developing system rather than a vocabulary assigned by one inventor.
shortlist.payoff: Understand emergence and regularization within a particular signing community without reducing sign language to gestures.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Documented cohort relationships and carefully sourced examples; no invented signs or unconsented portrayal of participants.
shortlist.principalRisk: Report-level evidence is broad; select one community later. Sign languages are full languages, not universal mime. Exact signing requires expertise, rights and consent; avoid deprivation spectacle.
shortlist.evidencePath: MPI research report (text accessed) and its listed primary field studies; later use community-aware scholarship and a specified cohort.
shortlist.historyComparison: No completed language story. Cycle #2’s Silbo reserve concerns whistled encoding of speech; emergence of a new signed system is distinct.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Individuals communicate → shared community → recurrent forms/structure across cohorts → explain regularization, not overnight invention.
researchRequirements: Choose a named community and retrieve primary longitudinal/cohort work.
Consult accurate linguistic description and culturally responsible examples.
Resolve signing expertise/rights; no fabricated documentary evidence.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Shortlist reserve: major domain expansion and human resonance; expertise and ethical asset needs are comparatively high.
preliminaryHooks: How does a language begin between people?

shortlist.title: The dice with no best die
shortlist.centralQuestion: How can A tend to beat B, B beat C, and C beat A?
shortlist.whyCare: Winning a pairwise comparison need not produce a universally best choice.
shortlist.payoff: Understand nontransitivity through transparent face-by-face probabilities rather than a trick reveal.
shortlist.visualOpportunity: Explicit dice faces and enumerated outcomes; keep illustrative probability separate from observed rolls.
shortlist.principalRisk: Probabilities require exact recomputation; dice must stay fixed and fair under the chosen model. Close conceptual adjacency to Cycle #1’s majority-cycle reserve; not a new voting research result.
shortlist.evidencePath: Quanta discovery explanation; later retrieve the original cited mathematical work and independently enumerate every outcome.
shortlist.historyComparison: No completed probability story. Billion Dollars is scale, not odds; prior unproduced majority-cycle is a meaningful structural overlap, transparently retained.
shortlist.conceptualArc: Assume a best die → pairwise comparisons → cycle → explain why ranking needs a specified opponent.
researchRequirements: Retrieve original dice examples/relevant mathematical source.
Enumerate probabilities independently and check fairness assumptions.
Distinguish elementary example from modern research generalizations.
shortlist.advancementJudgment: Shortlist reserve: compelling mental model; prior discovered cyclic-preference shape lowers freshness within this cycle.
preliminaryHooks: What if there is no best die?
